In p-type material **holes** are the majority carriers, so the minority carriers are
**free electrons**.
**Step 1 — see how p-type material is made.** Pure silicon or germanium is doped with
**trivalent** atoms - boron, aluminium, gallium or indium ✓ Each forms only three
covalent bonds and leaves a vacancy, a **hole**, which can move through the lattice.
**Step 2 — identify the majority carriers.** The holes, supplied in vast numbers by the
dopant ✓
**Step 3 — identify the minority carriers.** **Free electrons**, present only from the
**thermal** breaking of covalent bonds - the same process that occurs in the pure
material ✓
**How unequal the two populations are.** At room temperature in doped silicon:
holes: about **10²²** per cubic metre, set by the doping ✓
electrons: about **10¹⁰** per cubic metre ✓
a difference of **twelve orders of magnitude**.
**The law governing them.**
**np = n_i²** ✓
the product is fixed at a given temperature. Adding holes therefore **suppresses** the
electron population - which is why the minority carriers become so scarce.
**Why minority carriers matter at all.** They dominate the **reverse** current of a
diode and the leakage of a transistor ✓ Being thermally generated, they roughly
**double for every 10 °C** rise - which is why semiconductor devices become leaky when
hot.
**The n-type mirror image.** **Pentavalent** dopants - phosphorus, arsenic, antimony -
supply free **electrons** as majority carriers, leaving **holes** as the minority ✓
**Why the crystal stays neutral.** Each acceptor atom is neutral when added ✓ Once it
captures an electron it becomes a fixed **negative ion**, exactly balancing the mobile
positive hole. There are mobile positive carriers, but no net charge.
**What a hole really is.** Not a particle, but the **absence** of an electron in a
covalent bond ✓ It moves as neighbouring electrons shuffle into it, and behaves for all
practical purposes like a positive charge of mass comparable to the electron's.
**Reading the distractors.** **Holes** ✗ are the **majority** carriers here. **Both**
✗ ignores the distinction, and **neither** ✗ would describe an insulator ✓
∴ Free electrons.

Dynamic resistance is **ΔV/ΔI**; the micro prefix is the whole of the arithmetic.
**Step 1 — state the definition.**
r = ΔV/ΔI ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
r = 1/(0·5 x 10⁻⁶) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= 2 x 10⁶ Ω
= **2 MΩ** ✓
**Why the reverse resistance is so high.** Reverse bias **widens** the depletion region
and sweeps the majority carriers away from the junction ✓ The only current is the tiny
leakage of thermally generated **minority** carriers - microamps or less - so the
resistance is megohms.
**The contrast with forward bias.** There the resistance is typically **10 to 100 Ω** ✓
The ratio of reverse to forward resistance can exceed **10⁵**, and that enormous
asymmetry is what makes a diode a **rectifier**.
**Why the reverse current is nearly constant.** It is limited by the **rate of thermal
generation** of minority carriers, not by the voltage ✓ So the reverse characteristic
is almost flat, and the small 0·5 µA change over a whole volt reflects that.
**How temperature affects it.** The reverse current roughly **doubles every 10 °C** ✓
so the reverse resistance **halves** - which is why germanium diodes, with much larger
leakage than silicon, are rarely used in warm circuits.
**What happens at breakdown.** Beyond a critical reverse voltage the current rises
abruptly and the resistance **collapses** ✓ In a **Zener** diode this is deliberate and
reversible, and is used to regulate voltage.
**The arithmetic to watch.** 1/(0·5 x 10⁻⁶) = 2 x 10⁶ ✓ Dividing by a microamp
multiplies by a million, and then the 0·5 doubles it.
**A check by the other route.**
0·5 µA through 2 MΩ drops 0·5 x 10⁻⁶ x 2 x 10⁶ = **1 V** ✓ exactly the change stated.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 x 10⁵ Ω** ✗ is a factor of ten out. **200 Ω** ✗ would
be a typical **forward** resistance, and **2 Ω** ✗ is lower still ✓ Any answer below a
megohm is implausible for reverse bias.
∴ 2 × 10⁶ Ω.

Diffusion leaves the **n side positive** and the **p side negative**, so the p side sits
at the **lower** potential.
**Step 1 — follow the diffusion.** At the moment of contact, electrons diffuse from the
**n** side into the p, and holes from the **p** side into the n ✓
**Step 2 — see what is left behind.**
on the **n** side: fixed **positive** donor ions ✓
on the **p** side: fixed **negative** acceptor ions ✓
These immobile charges form the **depletion region**.
**Step 3 — read off the potentials.** Positive charge on the n side raises its
potential; negative charge on the p side lowers its ✓ So
**the potential at p is less than at n** ✓
**Step 4 — note the size of the step.** The **built-in potential** is about **0·7 V**
for silicon and **0·3 V** for germanium ✓
**Why the diffusion stops.** The growing field opposes further diffusion ✓ Equilibrium
is reached when the diffusion current exactly balances the drift current driven by that
field - and the barrier settles at its built-in value.
**Why the barrier cannot be measured with a voltmeter.** Connecting leads creates two
further metal-semiconductor junctions whose contact potentials exactly cancel the
barrier ✓ Otherwise an unbiased diode would be a free battery, in violation of the
second law of thermodynamics.
**What the barrier does.** It blocks further majority-carrier flow ✓ Forward bias
**lowers** it, and current flows freely; reverse bias **raises** it, and only leakage
remains.
**Why the fourth option is wrong even though it sounds similar.** "Potential at p is
+ve and at n is −ve" ✗ gets the **sign of the step the wrong way round**, and in any
case the absolute potentials depend on where the zero is chosen ✓ Only the
**difference** is physical.
**A useful picture.** Think of the depletion region as a small internal battery with
its **positive** terminal on the n side ✓ Forward bias means connecting an external
supply to oppose it.
**The depletion width.** Typically **0·5 µm**, narrowing under forward bias and
widening under reverse ✓ That variable width makes a reverse-biased junction a
voltage-controlled capacitor - the varactor.
∴ potential at p is less than that at n.

The two current gains are related by **α = β/(1 + β)**.
**Step 1 — recall the definitions.**
α = I_C/I_E, the **common-base** current gain ✓
β = I_C/I_B, the **common-emitter** current gain ✓
**Step 2 — use the current relation.** For a transistor,
I_E = I_B + I_C ✓
**Step 3 — derive the connection.** Dividing through by I_C:
I_E/I_C = I_B/I_C + 1
1/α = 1/β + 1 = (1 + β)/β
**α = β/(1 + β)** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
α = 100/101
= **0·990** ✓
**What α means physically.** The fraction of the emitter current that reaches the
collector ✓ Here **99%** of the injected carriers cross the thin base, and only 1% are
lost to recombination there - which is exactly what gives β = 100.
**Why α is always just below 1.** Some recombination in the base is unavoidable ✓ A
value of exactly 1 would mean a perfect transistor with infinite β.
**The inverse relation.**
β = α/(1 − α) ✓
which shows how sensitive β is: α = 0·99 gives β = 100, but α = 0·995 gives β = **199**.
A half-per-cent improvement in base transport doubles the current gain - and this
extreme sensitivity is why transistors from the same batch can have β varying by a
factor of three.
**Why the base is made thin and lightly doped.** To maximise α ✓ A thin base gives
carriers little chance to recombine, and light doping means few carriers of the
opposite type to recombine with.
**How circuits cope with the variability.** Good amplifier designs use **negative
feedback** so that the gain depends on resistor ratios rather than on β ✓
**A worked check.** With I_B = 1 mA and β = 100:
I_C = **100 mA**, I_E = **101 mA**
α = 100/101 = **0·990** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **1·01** ✗ exceeds 1, which α can never do - the collector
cannot receive more current than the emitter sends. **0·01** ✗ is 1 − α, the fraction
**lost** in the base. **100** ✗ is β itself ✓
∴ 0.99.

The output is 1 only when the inputs **differ** - the signature of the **XOR** gate.
**Step 1 — read the table row by row.**
A = 1, B = 0 → output **1** - inputs differ ✓
A = 1, B = 1 → output **0** - inputs same ✓
A = 0, B = 1 → output **1** - inputs differ ✓
A = 0, B = 0 → output **0** - inputs same ✓
**Step 2 — state the pattern.** The output is **1** exactly when the two inputs are
**unequal** ✓ That is the **exclusive-OR**.
**Step 3 — write the Boolean expression.**
Y = A ⊕ B = **A̅B + AB̅** ✓
**Why it is "exclusive".** An ordinary OR gives 1 when **either or both** inputs are 1 ✓
XOR **excludes** the both-ones case, which is the only row where it differs from OR -
and that single row is what the table turns on.
**Checking against the other gates.**
**OR**: 1,1 would give **1**, but the table says 0 ✗
**AND**: only 1,1 would give 1, so three rows are wrong ✗
**NOR**: only 0,0 would give 1 - the exact opposite of the table ✗
Only XOR matches all four rows ✓
**Where XOR is used.** It is the heart of the **half adder**: the sum bit of A + B is
A ⊕ B, and the carry is A·B ✓ Every arithmetic unit in every computer is built from
these.
**Its other uses.**
**parity** checking for error detection ✓
**comparison**: the output is 0 only when the inputs are equal
simple **encryption**, since XORing twice with the same key restores the original ✓
**controlled inversion**, where one input decides whether the other is passed or
inverted
**How to build one.** From four NAND gates, or as
Y = (A + B)·(A̅ + B̅) ✓ which is OR AND NAND - a standard exercise.
**The complement.** **XNOR** gives 1 when the inputs are the **same** ✓ and serves as
an equality detector.
∴ XOR.

Cooling makes a **metal** a better conductor and a **semiconductor** a worse one.
**Step 1 — take copper, a metal.** Its free-electron density is essentially **fixed**,
so the resistance is governed by the **collision rate** ✓ Cooling quietens the lattice
vibrations, the mean free time τ lengthens, and since
ρ = m/(ne²τ)
the resistivity **falls**. Copper's resistance **decreases** ✓
**Step 2 — take germanium, a semiconductor.** Its carriers must be **thermally
generated** across the band gap, with
n ∝ e^(−E_g/2kT) ✓
Cooling from 300 K to 100 K cuts that exponential drastically, and the loss of carriers
overwhelms any gain in mobility. Germanium's resistance **increases** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Germanium increases, copper decreases** ✓
**How large the semiconductor effect is.** For germanium, E_g = **0·67 eV** ✓ The
carrier concentration falls by a factor of order **10¹⁴** between 300 K and 100 K - the
crystal becomes effectively an **insulator**.
**The contrast in a sentence.** In a metal, cooling removes **obstacles**; in a
semiconductor, it removes **carriers** ✓
**The temperature coefficients.**
copper: α = **+0·004 K⁻¹**, positive ✓
germanium: **negative**, and strongly so ✓
**Where each behaviour is exploited.**
a **platinum resistance thermometer** uses the metal's steady positive coefficient ✓
a **thermistor** uses the semiconductor's steep negative one, for sensitive temperature
measurement and for inrush-current limiting ✓
**What happens to copper at very low temperatures.** The resistance flattens to a
**residual** value set by impurities and defects, which no amount of cooling removes ✓
Some metals - not copper - become **superconducting** and lose all resistance abruptly.
**A caution about mobility.** Cooling does **increase** the mobility in a semiconductor
too ✓ but that gain is utterly swamped by the exponential loss of carriers.
**Reading the distractors.** Any option with **germanium decreasing** ✗ treats it as a
metal; any with **copper increasing** ✗ treats it as a semiconductor ✓ The two must move
in opposite directions.
∴ Germanium increases, copper decreases.

p-type material needs a **trivalent** dopant, and of the four named only **gallium**
qualifies.
**Step 1 — check the valency of each dopant.**
**bismuth** - group 15, **pentavalent** ✗ donor, gives n-type
**antimony** - group 15, **pentavalent** ✗ donor, n-type
**gallium** - group 13, **trivalent** ✓ acceptor, gives **p-type**
**phosphorus** - group 15, **pentavalent** ✗ donor, n-type
**Step 2 — conclude.** Only **germanium doped with gallium** is p-type ✓
**Why a trivalent atom makes holes.** It has three valence electrons against the host's
four, so one covalent bond is left **incomplete** ✓ That vacancy - a **hole** - can
accept an electron from a neighbouring bond, and so migrates through the crystal as a
mobile positive carrier.
**Why a pentavalent atom makes electrons.** It has one electron **too many** for the
four bonds, and that extra electron is loosely held - about **0·01 eV** - so thermal
energy frees it at once ✓
**The mnemonic.** **P**entavalent gives **n**-type, and tri-valent gives **p**-type ✓
The letters are deliberately crossed, which is why it is worth fixing deliberately:
count the **valence electrons**, not the letters.
**Group 13 and group 15, in full.**
**trivalent acceptors**: boron, aluminium, **gallium**, indium ✓
**pentavalent donors**: phosphorus, arsenic, **antimony**, **bismuth** ✓
**The doping levels used.** About **one part in 10⁶ to 10⁸** ✓ enough to raise the
conductivity thousandfold while leaving the crystal structure untouched.
**Why germanium rather than silicon here.** Both work identically; germanium's smaller
band gap of 0·67 eV makes it more conductive but more temperature-sensitive ✓ Silicon,
at 1·1 eV, has displaced it almost everywhere in modern devices.
**What the doped crystal is like.** Still electrically **neutral**, with mobile holes
balanced by fixed negative acceptor ions ✓ and with electrons surviving as a tiny
minority population.
**Reading the distractors.** Bismuth, antimony and phosphorus ✗ are all pentavalent and
all give **n**-type material ✓ Only one option names a group-13 element.
∴ Germanium is doped with gallium.

Reverse bias **adds** to the built-in field and sweeps carriers away, so the depletion
region **widens**.
**Step 1 — recall what the depletion region is.** A zone around the junction stripped of
mobile carriers, containing only the **fixed** donor and acceptor ions ✓ Those ions
create the built-in potential barrier.
**Step 2 — apply reverse bias.** The n side is made **positive** and the p side
**negative** ✓ This pulls electrons further into the n region and holes further into
the p - **away** from the junction.
**Step 3 — see the consequence.** More ions are uncovered on each side, so the depletion
region **widens** ✓ and the barrier height **rises** from V₀ to V₀ + V.
**Step 4 — conclude.** The width is **increased by reverse bias** ✓
**What forward bias does.** The opposite: it pushes carriers **towards** the junction,
**narrowing** the depletion region and **lowering** the barrier ✓ Current then flows
freely.
**The quantitative law.**
w ∝ **√(V₀ + V)** for reverse bias ✓
so quadrupling the reverse voltage **doubles** the width - a square-root dependence, not
a linear one.
**Why this gives a capacitance.** A layer of fixed positive charge and one of fixed
negative charge, separated by an insulating gap - that is a **capacitor** ✓
C = εA/w, and since w grows with V, the capacitance **falls** as the reverse voltage
rises.
**The varactor diode.** A device designed to exploit exactly this ✓ Applying a control
voltage changes its capacitance, which tunes an LC circuit - the basis of electronic
tuning in radios, televisions and phase-locked loops.
**Why reverse current stays tiny.** The widened barrier blocks majority carriers
completely ✓ Only thermally generated **minority** carriers cross, giving the small,
nearly voltage-independent leakage.
**What happens if the reverse voltage is raised far enough.** **Breakdown** - either by
avalanche multiplication or by Zener tunnelling ✓ The current rises abruptly, and in a
Zener diode this is used deliberately to regulate voltage.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Increased by forward bias**" ✗ and "**decreased by
reverse bias**" ✗ both reverse the physics. "**Independent of bias**" ✗ would make the
varactor impossible ✓
∴ increased by reverse bias.

Amplification requires the **active** region: emitter junction **forward** biased,
collector junction **reverse** biased.
**Step 1 — see what each junction must do.**
the **emitter-base** junction must **inject** carriers into the base, which needs a
**low** barrier - hence **forward** bias ✓
the **collector-base** junction must **collect** them and keep the output current
independent of the output voltage, which needs a strong sweeping field - hence
**reverse** bias ✓
**Step 2 — conclude.** **Emitter-base forward, collector-base reverse** ✓
**Why this gives power gain.** The same current flows through a **low-resistance** input
and a **high-resistance** output ✓ Since P = I²R, the output power far exceeds the
input - and the extra energy comes from the d.c. supply, which the signal merely
controls.
**The current relations in the active region.**
I_E = I_B + I_C ✓
β = I_C/I_B, typically **100** ✓
α = I_C/I_E, typically **0·99**
A small base current controls a collector current a hundred times larger.
**Why the base must be thin and lightly doped.** So that **95 to 99%** of the injected
carriers cross it without recombining ✓ If the base were thick, most would recombine,
the collector would receive little, and there would be no gain at all.
**The four biasing regions.**
forward / reverse: **active** - linear amplification ✓
forward / forward: **saturation** - fully on, a closed switch ✓
reverse / reverse: **cut-off** - fully off, an open switch ✓
reverse / forward: **reverse active** - a poor amplifier, seldom used
Analogue circuits live in the active region; digital ones switch between saturation and
cut-off.
**How the biasing is arranged in practice.** A potential divider on the base, with an
emitter resistor for stability ✓ The aim is to place the **quiescent point** in the
middle of the active region so that the signal can swing both ways without clipping.
**Why the collector junction must not be forward biased.** The transistor would
saturate, the output would stop following the input, and the signal would be
**clipped** ✓ This is what happens when an amplifier is overdriven.
**Reading the distractors.** Each other option names saturation, cut-off or the
reverse-active mode ✓ none of which amplifies.
∴ emitter-base junction must be forward biased, collector-base junction must be reverse
biased.
